title: Ban the Scroll, Teach the Tool
author: EdTech Reframed
summary: This article critically examines the UK government's school phone ban policy in light of a University of Birmingham study finding that phone bans had no measurable effect on student mental wellbeing or academic attainment. The author argues that while bans may have some merit for reducing distraction, the research evidence does not support them as the primary response to the challenges of students and technology, and that the exclusive focus on restriction obscures the more important work of teaching digital literacy. The article makes a case for an approach that combines appropriate limitation of harmful scrolling behaviour with active instruction in how to use digital tools effectively and critically — 'ban the scroll, teach the tool' being its central thesis. Drawing on the distinction between passive consumption (algorithmically-driven, attention-extracting scrolling) and active, purposeful technology use, the author argues that students who have never been taught to use technology intentionally will not acquire that capacity from restriction alone. The piece is particularly relevant to school leaders and teachers developing technology policies who want to move beyond a binary of 'allow everything' or 'ban everything.'
points: University of Birmingham research on UK phone bans found no measurable improvement in wellbeing or attainment, challenging the assumption that restriction alone is sufficient as a technology policy.

The article distinguishes between harmful passive scrolling (algorithmically-driven, attention-extracting) and active, purposeful technology use — a distinction that phone bans treat as irrelevant by targeting devices rather than behaviors.

Digital literacy is not a skill students acquire by default once distractions are removed; without explicit instruction in intentional tool use, restriction creates a vacuum rather than developing capacity.

The 'ban the scroll, teach the tool' thesis argues for a both/and approach: restrict passive consumption in school settings while actively building students' capacity to use technology with purpose and critical awareness.

The strongest implication is that technology policy in schools needs a learning outcomes framework, not just a behavior management framework — the question is not only what to restrict but what students should be able to do with technology.

phyphox (Physical Phone Experiments), created at the 2nd Institute of Physics, RWTH Aachen University; free and open-source. Its experiment library includes worked, video-instructed examples such as Free Fall (timing a fall by acoustic or magnetic detection to find the gravitational acceleration g or the drop height), Elevator (using the phone’s pressure sensor to measure your speed and the height travelled), Pendulum, Sonar and Speed of Sound.
